Neither, to start with. The premise is the problem: more agents don't always give better results.

**Why it's tempting:** a team of ten specialists sounds better than one generalist. But each agent is a separate model call with its own context, and the agents have to pass information to each other. Anthropic's engineering team reports that agents use about 4× the tokens of a plain chat, and multi-agent systems about 15× ([Anthropic: how we built our multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)). I only saw excerpts of that post, so check the numbers there before you quote them at your review. With a small sponsor budget, that multiplier matters a lot.

**Worked example.** A student asks, "Can I book the laser cutter Friday at 3, and what material is safe?" One agent can look up the manual, check the calendar and book the slot, one step after another. Splitting that into a manual agent, a calendar agent, a booking agent and a coordinator adds three extra handoffs. Each handoff can drop detail, for example the exact time slot. It also adds model calls you pay for, and the answer isn't any better.

The same post says multi-agent setups pay off for tasks with heavy parallel work, information too big for one context window, or many complex tools. Your assistant has three narrow tools and short requests, so none of that applies yet.

**What I'd do:** start with one agent plus fixed steps where the order is always the same. Add a second agent only when you can name a concrete failure that one agent can't fix, such as a context that overflows or two jobs that really run at the same time. Then "five or ten" never comes up. You'd be able to say "one, because…" at your design review.

Quick check: a student asks about two different machines in one message. Is that a reason to split into agents? Why or why not?

If you want, I can turn this into a lesson on when splitting pays off.
